intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding malonyl-CoA decarboxylase (MLYCD, also called MCD).

checks.claim: Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MLYCD gene, which encodes malonyl-CoA decarboxylase.
checks.evidence_quote: We have identified two different homozygous mutations in human MCD (hMCD) by using RT-PCR analysis of fibroblast RNA from two previously reported consanguineous Scottish patients with MCD deficiency.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports causation by homozygous mutations only. It does not mention compound heterozygous mutations.

checks.claim: The gene encoding malonyl-CoA decarboxylase is called MLYCD, also known as MCD.

checks.explanation: The paper uses MCD. MLYCD is the approved symbol, so the claim only restates standard nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. Wightman et al. (2003) characterized it by malonic aciduria, developmental delay, seizure disorder, hypoglycemia, and cardiomyopathy. Gao et al. (1999) listed mild mental retardation, seizures, hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, vomiting, hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, and malonic aciduria as associated features.

They reported this patient as having a deficiency of malonyl-CoA decarboxylase, which they called a mitochondrial enzyme and an inborn error of metabolism not recognized before. The defect was first suspected because the child persistently excreted malonic and methylmalonic acids in the urine. Disturbances of lipid metabolism were also shown.

paragraphs.text: Haan et al. (1986) described a second child, a boy with a more severe deficiency of malonyl-CoA decarboxylase. He was mildly mentally retarded. During a urinary tract infection he presented with vomiting, a seizure, hypoglycemia, and mild metabolic acidosis. His urine contained increased amounts of malonic, methylmalonic, succinic, adipic, glutaric, and suberic acids. Mitochondrial malonyl-CoA decarboxylase activity in extracts of cultured fibroblasts was 4% of the mean control value.

paragraphs.text: MacPhee et al. (1993) described 2 new cases of malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, noting that until then the worldwide experience had been limited to 2 affected Australian children. The new patients were born in Scotland to consanguineous parents of Scottish/Irish origin. They were investigated during episodes of vomiting and febrile convulsions, together with developmental delay. Malonic aciduria and greatly reduced malonyl-CoA decarboxylase activity were demonstrated.

paragraphs.text: De Wit et al. (2006) described a girl with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency. Brain MRI showed white matter abnormalities together with diffuse pachygyria and periventricular heterotopia, consistent with a malformation of cortical development. The patient had a strikingly low appetite. The authors recommended that patients with the deficiency undergo brain MRI, and that unexplained malformations of cortical development prompt metabolic screening.

paragraphs.text: In the patient of Haan et al. (1986), a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet caused symptomatic hypoglycemia and moderate metabolic acidosis. On this diet the urine contained large amounts of the same organic acids and 3-hydroxybutyrate. On an isocaloric low-fat, high-carbohydrate diet, only relatively small amounts of malonic, methylmalonic, and succinic acid were excreted. Acute fat and lysine loads increased urinary excretion of malonic acid without changing excretion of the other organic acids. The authors concluded that malonyl-CoA decarboxylase prevents accumulation of malonyl-CoA in the mitochondrion, and that the enzyme matters most when fat is the main metabolic fuel.

paragraphs.text: FitzPatrick et al. (1999) used RT-PCR analysis of fibroblast RNA from the 2 consanguineous Scottish patients reported earlier by MacPhee et al. (1993). They found 2 different homozygous mutations in the MCD gene. One was a 442C-G transversion that creates a premature stop codon (S148X). The other was an intronic mutation (IVS4-14A-G) that creates a new splice acceptor site, causing a 13-bp insertion in the mature RNA and a frameshift with predicted protein truncation. Both mutations segregated appropriately within the families and were absent from 100 normal unrelated individuals.

paragraphs.text: Wightman et al. (2003) sequenced the genomic MLYCD gene in 9 unrelated patients and identified 16 of 18 pathogenic alleles. Western blot analysis of fibroblasts from 8 of these patients and from 2 previously reported patients with homozygous MLYCD mutations used antisera raised to a C-terminal peptide. A 66-kD band was absent in 6 patients and substantially reduced in 3; 1 patient had increased protein levels with a prominent smeary 68- to 83-kD band. Immunocytochemistry of patient cell lines that expressed MLYCD showed apparent intracellular mislocalization. The extreme N-terminal mutation c.8G-A (G3D) mislocalized the protein to the plasma membrane. A 25-base deletion between the putative mitochondrial and peroxisomal initiating codons (M1 and M40), and a point mutation that abolished the second of these (c.119T-C, M40T), both gave punctate perinuclear staining. None of these 3 mislocalizing mutations was predicted to alter catalytic function, so the authors proposed that correct subcellular localization of MLYCD is critical for its normal function.

paragraphs.text: FitzPatrick et al. (1999) found that the human MCD peptide has a C-terminal peroxisomal targeting sequence (-SKL). Subcellular fractionation of rat liver homogenates suggested that MCD is located in peroxisomes as well as mitochondria. Sacksteder et al. (1999) found MCD in both the cytoplasm and peroxisomes, and found MCD mRNA to be most abundant in cardiac and skeletal muscle. They proposed that cytoplasmic MCD regulates the abundance of cytoplasmic malonyl-CoA, and so the uptake and oxidation of fatty acids by mitochondria. They also proposed that peroxisomal MCD may break down malonyl-CoA produced inside peroxisomes by beta-oxidation of odd-chain-length dicarboxylic fatty acids.

paragraphs.text: FitzPatrick et al. (1999) found a homozygous intronic mutation (IVS4-14A-G) in the MCD gene in a consanguineous Scottish patient with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, previously reported by MacPhee et al. (1993). The mutation creates a new splice acceptor site. This causes a 13-bp insertion in the mature RNA and a frameshift with predicted protein truncation. The mutation segregated appropriately within the family and was absent from 100 normal unrelated individuals.

paragraphs.text: Wightman et al. (2003) found an extreme N-terminal c.8G-A mutation in the MLYCD gene, giving a gly3-to-asp (G3D) substitution, in a patient with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency. On immunocytochemistry the mutant protein was mislocalized to the plasma membrane. The authors suggested that a new targeting signal may lie in a conserved 4-amino acid N-terminal motif, and the mutation was not predicted to alter catalytic function.

paragraphs.text: Wightman et al. (2003) found a c.119T-C point mutation in the MLYCD gene, giving a met40-to-thr (M40T) substitution, in a patient with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency. The mutation abolishes the second of the putative mitochondrial and peroxisomal initiating codons (M40). On immunocytochemistry it showed punctate perinuclear staining, consistent with mislocalization, and it was not predicted to alter catalytic function.

agent.process_note: I read all 9 files in full. Eight are abstracts only and one (Chapel-Crespo et al., 2019) is a title only. I did not cite the title-only paper because it holds no substantive findings. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so the intro gives no gene MIM number or chromosome location. The gene (MCD/MLYCD) and recessive inheritance come from the abstracts of FitzPatrick et al. (homozygous mutations in consanguineous patients) and Wightman et al. (autosomal recessive). The abstracts did not give: the specific mutation found by Gao et al. (1999); the zygosity of the c.947-948delTT deletion (Sacksteder et al.); the zygosity of the Wightman et al. variants, or which patients carried them; and the ancestry of the Brown and Haan patients, apart from MacPhee et al. referring to the earlier cases as Australian children. I did not list the 25-base deletion from Wightman et al. as an allelic variant because the abstract does not give its position.
